paragraphs: The number of members the House of Representatives is to have is another very interesting point from which to consider this branch of the federal legislature. Hardly any article in the whole Constitution seems to deserve more attention, given the weight of character and the apparent force of argument with which it has been attacked. The charges brought against it are these. First, that so small a number of representatives will be an unsafe guardian of the public interests. Secondly, that they will lack proper knowledge of the local circumstances of their many constituents. Thirdly, that they will be drawn from the class of citizens who will sympathize least with the feelings of the mass of the people, and who will be most likely to aim at lifting the few permanently up by pushing the many down. Fourthly, that however inadequate the number will be at the start, it will grow more and more out of proportion as the people multiply and as obstacles prevent a matching increase in the representatives.

As a general matter, no political problem can be solved less precisely than the question of what number is most convenient for a representative legislature. And on no point do the policies of the individual States differ more, whether we compare their legislative assemblies directly with each other or consider the proportions they bear to the numbers of their constituents. Leave aside the difference between the smallest and largest States, such as Delaware, whose most numerous branch has twenty-one representatives, and Massachusetts, where it has between three and four hundred. A very considerable difference can still be seen among States of nearly equal population. Pennsylvania has no more than one fifth as many representatives as the State just mentioned. New York, whose population is to that of South Carolina as six to five, has little more than one third as many representatives. Georgia differs just as widely from Delaware or Rhode Island. In Pennsylvania the representatives are no more numerous than one for every four or five thousand constituents. In Rhode Island the proportion is at least one for every thousand. And under the constitution of Georgia, the proportion may reach one for every ten electors, and must unavoidably far exceed the proportion in any of the other States.

Another general remark is that the ratio between the representatives and the people should not be the same where the people are very numerous as where they are very few. If Virginia's representatives were set by Rhode Island's standard, they would now come to between four and five hundred, and in twenty or thirty years to a thousand. On the other hand, applying Pennsylvania's ratio to the State of Delaware would cut the latter's representative assembly to seven or eight members. Nothing is more misleading than to build our political calculations on arithmetical principles. Sixty or seventy men may more properly be trusted with a given degree of power than six or seven. But it does not follow that six or seven hundred would be proportionately a better guardian of it. And if we carry the supposition up to six or seven thousand, the whole reasoning ought to be reversed. The truth is that in all cases at least a certain number seems necessary to secure the benefits of free consultation and discussion and to guard against too easy a combination for improper purposes. On the other side, the number ought at most to be held within a certain limit, so as to avoid the confusion and intemperance of a multitude. In all very numerous assemblies, of whatever kind of people, passion never fails to wrest the scepter from reason. Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.

We must also recall here what was said about biennial elections. The limited powers of Congress and the control of the State legislatures justify less frequent elections than the public safety might otherwise demand. For the same reason, the members of Congress need not be as numerous as they would have to be if they held the whole power of legislation and were under no restraints beyond those ordinarily placed on other legislative bodies.

With these general ideas in mind, let us weigh the objections raised against the number of members proposed for the House of Representatives. It is said, first, that so small a number cannot safely be trusted with so much power.

This branch of the legislature will have sixty-five members when the government begins. Within three years a census is to be taken, and then the number may be raised to one for every thirty thousand inhabitants. The census is to be renewed within every following period of ten years, and increases may continue to be made under the same limit. It will not be thought an extravagant guess that the first census will raise the number of representatives, at the rate of one for every thirty thousand, to at least one hundred. If the negroes are counted at three fifths, there can hardly be any doubt that the population of the United States will by then amount to three millions, if it does not already. At the end of twenty-five years, at the computed rate of increase, the number of representatives will come to two hundred, and at the end of fifty years to four hundred. I presume this number will put an end to all fears arising from the smallness of the body. I take for granted here what I shall show later, in answering the fourth objection: that the number of representatives will be increased from time to time in the way the Constitution provides. On the opposite supposition, I should admit that the objection carries very great weight indeed.

The true question to be decided, then, is whether the smallness of the number, as a temporary regulation, endangers the public liberty. Is sixty-five members for a few years, and a hundred or two hundred for a few more, a safe guardian for a limited and well-guarded power of legislating for the United States? I must own that I could not answer no without first wiping out every impression I have received of the present character of the people of America, of the spirit that moves the State legislatures, and of the principles woven into the political character of every class of citizens. I cannot conceive that the people of America, in their present disposition, or under any circumstances that can soon arise, will choose, and every second year choose again, sixty-five or a hundred men who would be inclined to form and carry out a scheme of tyranny or treachery. I cannot conceive that the State legislatures, which must feel so many motives to watch the federal legislature and have so many means of counteracting it, would fail to detect or to defeat a conspiracy by the latter against the liberties of their common constituents. I am equally unable to conceive that there are now, or can be within any short time, in the United States any sixty-five or a hundred men able to win the choice of the people at large who would either wish or dare, in the short space of two years, to betray the solemn trust committed to them. What change of circumstances, time and a fuller population of our country may bring about would take a prophetic spirit to declare, and I make no claim to one. But judging from the circumstances now before us, and from their probable state within a moderate period of time, I must pronounce that the liberties of America cannot be unsafe in the number of hands the federal Constitution proposes.

Where can the danger come from? Are we afraid of foreign gold? If foreign gold could so easily corrupt our federal rulers and enable them to ensnare and betray their constituents, how is it that we are a free and independent nation today? The Congress that led us through the Revolution was a less numerous body than their successors will be. They were not chosen by their fellow citizens at large, nor answerable to them. Though they were appointed from year to year and could be recalled at pleasure, they were generally kept on for three years, and before the ratification of the federal articles for a still longer term. They always held their consultations in secrecy. They alone conducted our affairs with foreign nations. Throughout the whole course of the war they held the fate of their country more in their hands than it is to be hoped our future representatives ever will. And given the greatness of the prize at stake and the eagerness of the party that lost it, we may well suppose that means other than force would not have been scrupled. Yet we know from happy experience that the public trust was not betrayed, and the purity of our public councils in this respect has never suffered, even from the whispers of slander.

Is the danger feared from the other branches of the federal government? But where will the President, or the Senate, or both, find the means? Their pay for office, it is to be presumed, will not exceed what is needed for very different purposes, and without first corrupting the House of Representatives it cannot. Their private fortunes, since they must all be American citizens, cannot possibly be sources of danger. The only means they can have, then, lie in handing out appointments. Is it here that suspicion rests her charge? Sometimes we are told that the President is to use up this fund of corruption in subduing the virtue of the Senate. Now it is the fidelity of the other House that is to be the victim. The improbability of such a mercenary and treacherous combination among the several members of the government should alone quiet this fear. They stand on foundations as different as republican principles will well allow, and they are at the same time accountable to the society over which they are placed. But fortunately the Constitution has provided a still further safeguard. The members of Congress are made ineligible to any civil offices that may be created, or whose emoluments may be increased, during the term for which they were elected. No offices, therefore, can be handed out to the sitting members except those that fall vacant by ordinary chance. To suppose that these would be enough to buy the guardians of the people, chosen by the people themselves, is to give up every rule by which events ought to be calculated, and to put in its place an indiscriminate and unbounded jealousy, against which all reasoning must be useless. The sincere friends of liberty who surrender themselves to the extravagances of this passion do not realize the injury they do their own cause. There is a degree of depravity in mankind that calls for a certain degree of caution and distrust; but there are other qualities in human nature that justify a certain portion of esteem and confidence. Republican government presupposes these qualities in a higher degree than any other form does. If the pictures that the political jealousy of some among us has drawn were faithful likenesses of the human character, the inference would be that men do not have enough virtue for self-government, and that nothing less than the chains of despotism can keep them from destroying and devouring one another.
